notes: 'The old man asked the Emperor for help. He sent many men to the house.' - 'He' could be read as the old man for a moment; consider 'The Emperor sent many men to the house.'

'His men took the drink up Mount Fuji. There, they burned it.' - burning a drink is slightly odd for a beginner; consider 'They put the drink in a big fire on Mount Fuji.' or mention the letter too, as in A2.
'At once' appears three times; it is A2-ish. 'right away' or simply dropping it would be safer for A1. 'At once, her heart changed.' could become 'At once, she was not sad any more.'
Three different robes appear (suitor's robe, Kaguya's robe, the moon robe); 'a robe from the moon' (as in A2) would help readers keep them apart.

'The first man brought an old bowl, but it had no light.' - the reader was never told the bowl should shine; consider 'Kaguya wanted a holy bowl with a light in it. The first man brought an old bowl, but it had no light.'
'The last man also came back with nothing.' - he did not travel anywhere; 'The last man also brought nothing.' is cleaner.

issues.quote: He secretly paid workers to make one. But then they came to the house and asked for their money.
issues.problem: If he paid the workers, there is no reason for them to come and ask for their money; the sentence contradicts the next one and the original (he never paid the craftsmen), and B2/C1 say they demanded unpaid wages.
issues.fix: He secretly asked workers to make one, but he never paid them. When he brought the branch to the house, the workers came too and asked for their money.

notes: 'He only took an old bowl from a mountain temple, and it did not shine.' - the text never says the real bowl should shine; add 'The real bowl was supposed to shine with holy light.'
'This suitor set sail himself' - 'himself' implies he first sent others, which B2 does not mention (C1 does); either drop 'himself' or add a clause about his servants running off.
'a robe made from the fur of the fire rat, which could not be burned' - 'which' could attach to the rat; 'a robe of fire-rat fur that no flame could burn' is cleaner.
'sit near the edge of the house in the evenings' is a slightly odd rendering of the veranda; 'sit out on the veranda' reads more naturally.

summary: A faithful, age-appropriate retelling of the Tale of the Bamboo Cutter across all five levels, with correct quiz keys and well-controlled grammar. B1 fails on one concrete contradiction: the second suitor 'paid' the workers who then come asking for their money. A1, A2, B2 and C1 pass with only minor notes.
